channel.title: CircleCI runner job wrapper – Documentation
channel.description: Recent content in Documentation on CircleCI runner job wrapper

item.title: Configuration
item.description:
All settings are environment variables of the runner process. They reach the wrapper because the runner passes its environment on. Five of them can also be KEY=value lines in the operator file (CCI_JOBLOG_CONF), marked file below. The file supplies defaults and the environment wins.

Variable Default Meaning
CCI_JOBLOG_FILE /var/log/circleci-job-wrapper/jobs.jsonl JSONL output file. The directory is created if missing. Skipped silently if unwritable
CCI_JOBLOG_STATE_DIR /run/circleci-job-wrapper Directory for the <runner>.json current-job files
CCI_JOBLOG_STATE_ON_END remove remove deletes the state file at job end. idle rewrites it as {"state":"idle",...}
CCI_JOBLOG_HOST_CACHE /run/circleci-job-wrapper/host.env Host identity cache (key=value)
CCI_JOBLOG_CONF /etc/circleci-job-wrapper/wrapper.env Operator file. Parsed, never sourced
CCI_JOBLOG_IMDS_URL http://169.254.169.254 Metadata endpoint. Override for tests
CCI_RUNNER_CONFIG the parent’s --config, else /etc/circleci-runner/circleci-runner-config.yaml Runner config to read runner.name from
CCI_RUNNER_NAME from the runner config Runner name. Wins over the config file (file)
CCI_RESOURCE_CLASS empty Resource class (file)
CCI_JOBLOG_EXTRA_FIELDS empty k=v,k=v, merged into every event as strings (file). Reserved names and keys containing token, secret, passw, credential, auth or apikey are skipped. 128 bytes per value
CCI_JOBLOG_APP_URL https://app.circleci.com Base for workflow_url and pipeline_url. Set it for CircleCI Server
CCI_JOBLOG_PROM_DIR empty (off) Write <dir>/<runner>.prom, a Prometheus textfile with the busy gauge (file)
CCI_JOBLOG_PROM_JOB_ID empty 1 adds job_id and workflow_id labels to the busy gauge (file). One series per job: fine for small fleets, high cardinality otherwise
CCI_JOBLOG_HTTP_URL empty (off) POST every event here, in the background, with --max-time 2
CCI_JOBLOG_HTTP_HEADER empty One extra header, for example Authorization: Bearer .... Passed to curl on stdin, so it is not visible in ps
CCI_JOBLOG_FORWARD_SIGNALS 1 0 stops the wrapper forwarding TERM, INT and HUP to the agent
CCI_JOBLOG_DISABLE empty Non-empty: exec the agent directly, with no telemetry. A kill switch
CCI_JOBLOG_DEBUG empty Non-empty: diagnostics on stderr. Never secrets, never agent arguments

Runner name

The wrapper uses the first of these:

  1. CCI_RUNNER_NAME, or the operator file.
  2. The name: key directly under the top-level runner: key of the runner config. The config is CCI_RUNNER_CONFIG, else the --config <file> argument of the parent runner process, else /etc/circleci-runner/circleci-runner-config.yaml.

A tiny parser extracts only that one value. The api: and auth token lines are never stored, logged or used. With no name, the state file is called pid-<runner pid>.json.

Resource class

The runner config does not contain the resource class (the token maps to it), and the runner passes none in the job environment. Set it in the operator file:

# /etc/circleci-job-wrapper/wrapper.env (one file per host; not sourced)
CCI_RESOURCE_CLASS=my-org/linux-large
CCI_JOBLOG_EXTRA_FIELDS=team=infra,pool=bazel

With several runners of different resource classes on one host, set CCI_RESOURCE_CLASS and CCI_RUNNER_NAME in each runner’s service environment instead. resolve_runner_and_class in the script has a marked HOOK for reading the class from a CIRCLE_* variable, should a future runner provide one.

Busy gauge

With CCI_JOBLOG_PROM_DIR set, the wrapper also writes <dir>/<runner>.prom, a Prometheus textfile:

circleci_runner_busy{runner,resource_class,instance_id[,job_name,project,job_id,workflow_id]} 1|0
circleci_runner_job_start_time_seconds{...} # only while busy

job_name and project are present while busy. CCI_JOBLOG_PROM_JOB_ID=1 adds job_id and workflow_id, one series per job, so use it on small fleets only. Read the file with Alloy’s prometheus.exporter.unix textfile collector or node_exporter’s --collector.textfile.directory.

State file

<CCI_JOBLOG_STATE_DIR>/<runner-name-or-pid>.json (name sanitised to [A-Za-z0-9._-]) is written atomically (temp file and mv) at job start and removed at job end. It has the same fields as job_start, plus "state":"running" and "updated_at".

A wrapper that is SIGKILLed cannot clean up, so treat a file whose wrapper_pid is no longer alive as stale. /run is tmpfs, so stale files vanish at reboot.

Logrotate

logrotate/circleci-job-wrapper rotates daily, keeps 7 compressed files and uses copytruncate. The wrapper opens the file with O_APPEND for every event, so truncating in place is safe for any number of concurrent appenders. At worst, the lines written between logrotate’s copy and truncate are lost.

create would hand the new file to root and silently stop every runner account from logging, because the wrapper never fails a job over logging. For lossless rotation, use create 0664 <runner-user> <runner-group> instead.

item.title: Event schema
item.description:
The wrapper writes one JSON object per line (schema version 1), UTF-8. Each line is written with a single append and stays well under 4 KiB, so concurrent appends from many runner agents do not interleave.

All identifiers are strings, and a missing value is "", so every line has the same keys. job_end additionally has agent_exit_code, duration_ms, start_ms, end_ms, cpu_user_ms, cpu_sys_ms and agent_status.

Field Source
schema (number), event, ts job_start or job_end. ts is RFC 3339 UTC with milliseconds
job_id CIRCLE_WORKFLOW_JOB_ID (fallback CIRCLE_JOB_ID). The join key: equals com.circleci.job.id on CircleCI spans
job_name, job_number CIRCLE_JOB, CIRCLE_BUILD_NUM
workflow_id, pipeline_id CIRCLE_WORKFLOW_ID, CIRCLE_PIPELINE_ID
trace_id The pipeline ID without dashes. It is the trace ID of CircleCI’s OpenTelemetry spans, so it joins an event to its trace
cgroup The runner agent’s cgroup, read from /proc/self/cgroup, for example /system.slice/circleci-runner.service. It joins cAdvisor per-service metrics. An agent runs one job at a time, so the series is per job
pipeline_number CIRCLE_PIPELINE_NUMBER. The runner does not provide it, so it is normally empty
workflow_url, pipeline_url <base>/workflow/<workflow_id> and <base>/pipeline/<pipeline_id>. The base is CCI_JOBLOG_APP_URL
project, org CIRCLE_PROJECT_REPONAME, CIRCLE_PROJECT_USERNAME
org_id, project_id CIRCLE_ORGANIZATION_ID, CIRCLE_PROJECT_ID
branch, sha, build_url, node_index CIRCLE_BRANCH, CIRCLE_SHA1, CIRCLE_BUILD_URL (the job link), CIRCLE_NODE_INDEX
pr_number CIRCLE_PR_NUMBER. The runner does not provide it, so it is normally empty
hostname The host’s name
instance_id, instance_type, availability_zone, region, private_ip, ami_id EC2 instance identity document. Empty off EC2
runner_name, resource_class See Configuration
wrapper_pid, agent_pid (numbers) The wrapper and the task agent process
extra fields CCI_JOBLOG_EXTRA_FIELDS
agent_exit_code, duration_ms, start_ms, end_ms (numbers), agent_status job_end only. start_ms and end_ms are epoch milliseconds
cpu_user_ms, cpu_sys_ms (numbers) job_end only. CPU time of the job’s whole process tree, from the reaped-children rusage of the wrapper in /proc/<pid>/stat. It assumes CLK_TCK=100, standard on Linux x86_64 and arm64

agent_status is completed (the agent exited 0), agent_error, or cancelled (the wrapper received TERM, INT or HUP). It describes the agent process, not the job result. See How it works.

Only the variables listed here are ever read. The environment is never dumped and the agent’s command line is never logged. The CIRCLE_* names are read defensively, and any that the runner does not provide are empty.

Example 

{"schema":1,"event":"job_start","ts":"2026-11-18T20:31:55.456Z","job_id":"5b1e0c1a-0000-4000-8000-000000000001","job_name":"build","job_number":"1234","workflow_id":"7f3d0000-0000-4000-8000-000000000002","workflow_url":"https://app.circleci.com/workflow/7f3d0000-0000-4000-8000-000000000002","pipeline_id":"a1b20000-0000-4000-8000-000000000003","pipeline_url":"https://app.circleci.com/pipeline/a1b20000-0000-4000-8000-000000000003","pipeline_number":"","project":"example-repo","org":"example-org","org_id":"c0de0000-0000-4000-8000-000000000004","project_id":"d00d0000-0000-4000-8000-000000000005","branch":"main","sha":"0123456789abcdef0123456789abcdef01234567","build_url":"https://app.circleci.com/jobs/1234","node_index":"0","pr_number":"","hostname":"ip-10-0-1-23","instance_id":"i-0123456789abcdef0","instance_type":"c7g.xlarge","availability_zone":"us-east-1b","region":"us-east-1","private_ip":"10.0.1.23","ami_id":"ami-0abc1234def567890","runner_name":"runner-1","resource_class":"my-org/linux-large","wrapper_pid":1656458,"agent_pid":1656459,"team":"infra","pool":"bazel"}
{"schema":1,"event":"job_end","ts":"2026-11-18T20:31:55.758Z","job_id":"5b1e0c1a-0000-4000-8000-000000000001","job_name":"build","...":"(same fields as job_start)","team":"infra","pool":"bazel","agent_exit_code":0,"duration_ms":302,"start_ms":1795033915456,"end_ms":1795033915758,"agent_status":"completed"}

The "...": key in the second line only abbreviates this page. Real lines repeat all fields.

item.title: Example Grafana dashboard
item.description:
examples/grafana/build_dashboard.py generates the dashboard JSON. Pass the datasource UIDs of your stack:

python3 examples/grafana/build_dashboard.py --prom <prom-uid> --loki <loki-uid> --tempo <tempo-uid> > dashboard.json
# upload: POST /api/dashboards/db with {"dashboard": <dashboard.json>, "overwrite": true}

For CircleCI Server, also pass --app-url so the links point at your installation. The dashboard needs the Alloy example data, and the CircleCI spans for the span panels.

Tour of the dashboards

Follow one path from the fleet down to a single job, a runner and a resource class. Every dashboard links to the next, so you rarely type a variable by hand.

1. Pipeline performance

The top of the fleet dashboard, from CircleCI spans: workflows, success rate, median and P95 wall time, workflows by result, the slowest jobs and recent workflows. Use the branch filter to compare branches, then scroll down to see which runners did the work.

2. The fleet right now

Busy and idle runners, and what each runner is running now, from the busy gauge. Click a runner name to open its runner detail, a job ID to open the job detail, or a job name to open the job in CircleCI.

3. Jobs per host

Jobs per host, job results per host, and failed jobs per host over time. A spike of failures on one host is a wedged worker. Live step activity shows what the task agent is doing. Click a host or a job to go deeper.

4. The job trace

Job detail. The top shows where and when the job ran (EC2 instance, runner, cgroup) and the CircleCI job result. Below is the full trace timeline: pipeline, workflow, job and steps. Scroll down for the steps and resources.

5. Steps and the resources the job used

Steps, slowest first, each with its step status (ok or failed, from the span status) and its exit code, from CircleCI step spans. Next are the live step progress from the task agent log, and the job’s own CPU and memory (the runner’s cgroup) with the CPU time the job used. A slow step with high CPU is compute-bound. A slow step with low CPU is waiting.

6. The runner

Runner detail, reached by clicking a runner name. It shows status, jobs taken, failures, busy percentage, CPU time, the runner’s CPU and memory, and jobs and results over time. Click the resource class to see the whole class.

7. The resource class

Resource class: runners, busy now, utilization, job counts and P50 and P95 durations, the runners in the class and the load per runner. Use it to decide whether the class needs more or fewer runners.

Fleet dashboard

The runner fleet dashboard (uid cci-runner-fleet), from a small test fleet.

Rows, top to bottom:

  • Pipeline performance (CircleCI spans). Workflows, success rate, median and P95 wall time, workflows by result, slowest jobs (median, P95, max) and recent workflows with links. Tested on Grafana Cloud Tempo with TraceQL metrics.
  • Fleet right now. Busy and idle runners, hosts reporting, and a table of what each runner is doing (job, project, running for), from the busy gauge.
  • Host health per instance: CPU, IO wait, memory, disk, network and load, with job starts as annotations.
  • Jobs per host. Jobs started per host, job results from the task-agent log and from CircleCI spans, failed jobs over time (a spike on one host is a wedged worker) and live step activity from the task-agent journal.
  • Recent jobs. Which host ran what.

Job, workflow and pipeline IDs link to the CircleCI UI (build_url, workflow_url, pipeline_url). Drill into this job opens the job-detail dashboard for that job.

Job-detail dashboard

examples/grafana/build_job_dashboard.py generates it (uid cci-runner-job). Open it from the fleet dashboard, or with ?var-job_id=<id>&var-trace_id=<pipeline id without dashes>&var-cgroup=<wrapper cgroup>&var-instance=<instance id> plus a time range.

The job-detail dashboard for one job.

  • Where and when it ran, from the wrapper, and the result, from the CircleCI job span.
  • The full trace timeline: pipeline, workflow, job and steps.
  • Steps, slowest first, from step spans, with each step’s step status (ok or failed, from the span status) and exit code (com.circleci.step.exit_code).
  • Live step progress as it happened, from the task-agent log on the host (experimental).
  • Job CPU and memory of the runner’s service cgroup, from cAdvisor via the Alloy example.
  • CPU time of the job (cpu_user_ms, cpu_sys_ms) from the wrapper.
  • Host metrics during the job window.

More dashboards (runner detail, resource class detail) are being added to examples/grafana/.

Runner detail dashboard

examples/grafana/build_runner_dashboards.py runner generates it (uid cci-runner-detail). Click any runner name in the other dashboards, or open it with ?var-runner=<runner name>. The cgroup and instance variables fill in from the runner’s busy gauge.

  • Summary: status now, jobs taken, failed jobs, share of time busy, CPU time used by its jobs, and median job duration.
  • Running now: the current job, with links to CircleCI and to the job-detail dashboard.
  • Resources: the runner service’s own CPU and memory (cAdvisor, its cgroup), its busy/idle state, and the host’s CPU, IO wait and memory.
  • Jobs this runner took: jobs over time, results over time (task agent log, experimental), duration per job, and a table of every job, newest first, linked to CircleCI and to the job-detail dashboard.

Failed-job counts come from the task agent’s journal line, matched to the runner through its systemd unit (label_format cg="/system.slice/{{.unit}}"), so they need the optional journal pipeline in the Alloy example.

Resource class dashboard

examples/grafana/build_runner_dashboards.py resource-class generates it (uid cci-runner-rc). Click any resource class in the other dashboards, or open it with ?var-rc=<namespace>/<class>.

  • Summary: runners, busy now, utilization over the time range, jobs, and median and P95 job duration (CircleCI spans filtered on com.circleci.resource.class).
  • Runners in this class: busy or idle, the current job, and CPU now; each runner links to its detail dashboard.
  • Capacity and load: busy runners against runners, jobs started per runner, job results, host CPU for the hosts in the class, and CPU and memory per runner.
  • Jobs in this class: slowest jobs (median, P95, max) and recent jobs.

Queue depth and wait time per class are not in these dashboards: CircleCI’s spans don’t carry them. The fleet API (GET /api/v3/runner/fleets, or circleci runner fleet list) returns running and queued counts per class if you want to poll them.

Upload all four 

for d in fleet job runner resource-class; do
 case $d in
 fleet) python3 examples/grafana/build_dashboard.py ;;
 job) python3 examples/grafana/build_job_dashboard.py ;;
 *) python3 examples/grafana/build_runner_dashboards.py "$d" ;;
 esac > "$d.json"
 jq -n --slurpfile d "$d.json" '{dashboard: $d[0], overwrite: true}' |
 curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $GRAFANA_TOKEN" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
 -X POST "$GRAFANA_URL/api/dashboards/db" -d @-
done

All four accept --prom, --loki, --tempo (data source UIDs) and --app-url (CircleCI UI base, for CircleCI Server).

item.title: Join data with CircleCI OpenTelemetry
item.description:
CircleCI’s own OpenTelemetry job, step and task spans carry com.circleci.resource.class and com.circleci.job.status, but no runner or host identity. They are sent when each job finishes. The wrapper and the host agents add the where and the live view. Everything joins on a few keys: job_id, trace_id (the pipeline ID without dashes, the trace ID of the spans), instance_id and cgroup. The end-to-end guide shows how to turn the export on.

Source Carries Join key
Wrapper events (jobs.jsonl) job_id, workflow_id, instance_id, runner_name, resource_class, start and end job_id = CIRCLE_WORKFLOW_JOB_ID
CircleCI spans (OTLP exporter) Job result (com.circleci.job.status), resource class, step spans and durations com.circleci.job.id = job_id
Host metrics (Alloy unix exporter, textfile busy gauge) CPU, memory, disk, network, busy or idle per runner instance_id label
Task-agent journal (optional, experimental) Step start and end, the job result as the host sees it, in near real time job-id = job_id, plus instance_id 
flowchart LR
WE["Wrapper events"] -->|job_id| ONE["One job: where it ran, when, result, steps, CPU and memory"]
SP["CircleCI spans"] -->|com.circleci.job.id| ONE
TA["Task agent log"] -->|job-id| ONE
HM["Host and runner metrics"] -->|instance_id, cgroup| ONE

To receive the spans, add an exporter in the organization settings or with CircleCI’s exporter API (POST /api/v2/otel/exporters). See Set it up end to end for the UI and API steps, and Ship with Grafana Alloy for a worked example, and CircleCI’s documentation for the current API.

item.title: Set it up end to end
item.description:
This is the one install path. It takes you from nothing to a dashboard where you pick a CircleCI job and see its trace, its steps, the host it ran on and the CPU it used. Do the stages in order. Each stage says why you do it, what to do, and how to check that it worked before you go on.

Stages 1 to 3 are the wrapper alone, and are enough to get host identity on every job. Stages 4 to 7 add CircleCI spans, a shipper and the dashboards. For several runners on one host, upgrades and removal, see Several runners, upgrades and removal.

flowchart LR
W["Job wrapper<br/>(runner command_prefix)"] -->|job events| L[("jobs.jsonl")]
T["Task agent"] -->|steps, result| J[("Runner journal")]
M["Host and runner<br/>metrics"]
L --> AL["Grafana Alloy"]
J --> AL
M --> AL
AL -->|OTLP| G[("Grafana Cloud")]
C["CircleCI<br/>OpenTelemetry export"] -->|spans| G
G --> D["Dashboards"]

Note

This is a CircleCI Labs project, not an official CircleCI product. Pages mark what is tested and what is not.

What gets installed

Stage What Where Needed for
2 circleci-job-wrapper /usr/local/bin/ Everything
2 Log directory /var/log/circleci-job-wrapper/ Everything
2 Host cache unit /etc/systemd/system/circleci-job-wrapper-hostcache.service EC2 identity without a metadata call per job
2 Log rotation /etc/logrotate.d/circleci-job-wrapper Daily rotation of jobs.jsonl
2 Operator file /etc/circleci-job-wrapper/wrapper.env Resource class, busy gauge
3 command_prefix line /etc/circleci-runner/circleci-runner-config.yaml Turns the wrapper on
4 OpenTelemetry exporter CircleCI organization settings Job result, steps, timing
5 Grafana Alloy config /etc/alloy/config.alloy Shipping data to your backend
6 Dashboards Grafana Seeing it all

1. Prerequisites

Why: the wrapper needs a modern machine runner and a few standard tools, and you need the rights to finish stages 4 to 7. Finding a gap now is cheaper than finding it in stage 5.

Do: confirm you have all of these.

  • A CircleCI machine runner 3.1.11 or later on Linux. Tested with 3.1.14 on Ubuntu 24.04.
  • Organization admin rights in CircleCI, to add an OpenTelemetry exporter (stage 4).
  • On EC2, the instance metadata service (IMDS) enabled. IMDSv2 works. Off EC2 the EC2 fields stay empty and nothing else changes.
  • bash 4 or later, curl, and shell access with sudo to the runner host.
  • For stages 4 to 7: a Grafana Cloud stack (or another OTLP backend) and a Grafana access token.

Check 1a: the runner is installed and running. This proves the runner agent the wrapper will wrap exists, is up, and is a supported version. On the runner host:

systemctl is-active circleci-runner
circleci-runner --version

Expected output:

active
circleci-runner version 3.1.14-10146-3ce7306 (built 2026-10-20T23:31:41Z)

Any version from 3.1.11 up is fine.

If it fails: if the service is not active or the version is older, see Troubleshooting and upgrade the runner first. If your unit has another name, use that name here and in later stages.

Check 1b: the host can reach the EC2 metadata service. This proves the wrapper can fill instance_id and instance_type on every event. On the runner host:

# IMDSv2: ask for a short-lived token, then use it
TOKEN=$(curl -s -X PUT \
 -H 'X-aws-ec2-metadata-token-ttl-seconds: 60' \
 http://169.254.169.254/latest/api/token)
curl -s -H "X-aws-ec2-metadata-token: $TOKEN" \
 http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/instance-id

Expected output:

i-0123456789abcdef0

Off EC2 you can skip this check: the EC2 fields stay empty and nothing else changes.

If it fails: an empty reply usually means IMDS is disabled or the hop limit is too low for your setup, see EC2 fields are empty.

Check 1c: the tools are present. This proves the wrapper’s only dependencies exist. On the runner host:

bash --version | head -1
curl --version | head -1

Expected output:

GNU bash, version 5.2.21(1)-release (x86_64-pc-linux-gnu)
curl 8.5.0 (x86_64-pc-linux-gnu) libcurl/8.5.0 OpenSSL/3.0.13

Any bash 4 or later passes.

If it fails: install bash 4 or later and curl with your package manager.

2. Install the wrapper

Why: this puts the wrapper script, its log directory and its host cache on the host, so that a job can be recorded.

Do: on every host that runs a runner agent, from a checkout of this repository. Replace circleci with the account and group your runner runs as.

On the runner host:

# the wrapper
sudo install -m 0755 bin/circleci-job-wrapper \
 /usr/local/bin/circleci-job-wrapper
# the log directory: the runner user must be able to write it
sudo install -d -m 0775 -o root -g circleci \
 /var/log/circleci-job-wrapper

# boot-time host cache (EC2 identity without a call per job)
sudo install -m 0644 \
 systemd/circleci-job-wrapper-hostcache.service \
 /etc/systemd/system/
sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo systemctl enable --now \
 circleci-job-wrapper-hostcache.service

# daily log rotation
sudo install -m 0644 logrotate/circleci-job-wrapper \
 /etc/logrotate.d/circleci-job-wrapper

Then write the operator file. It is parsed, never sourced. On the runner host:

sudo install -d /etc/circleci-job-wrapper
sudo tee /etc/circleci-job-wrapper/wrapper.env >/dev/null <<'ENV'
CCI_RESOURCE_CLASS=my-org/linux-large
CCI_JOBLOG_PROM_DIR=/run/circleci-job-wrapper/prom
CCI_JOBLOG_PROM_JOB_ID=1
ENV
  • CCI_RESOURCE_CLASS is your resource class. The runner does not tell the wrapper, so set it here.
  • CCI_JOBLOG_PROM_DIR turns on the Prometheus busy gauge (a live busy or idle view per runner). Optional, but the fleet dashboard uses it.
  • CCI_JOBLOG_PROM_JOB_ID=1 adds job_id and workflow_id labels to the gauge, one series per job. Fine for small fleets. Optional.

Check 2a: the host cache is running and holds the instance ID. This proves later jobs get EC2 identity from a file instead of a metadata call. On the runner host:

systemctl is-active circleci-job-wrapper-hostcache.service
grep instance_id /run/circleci-job-wrapper/host.env

Expected output:

active
instance_id=i-0123456789abcdef0

If it fails: see EC2 fields are empty. Off EC2, active alone is enough.

Check 2b: the wrapper script parses. This proves the copy on disk is intact. On the runner host:

bash -n /usr/local/bin/circleci-job-wrapper && echo ok

Expected output:

ok

If it fails: install the script again from the checkout. Settings are in Configuration.

3. Configure the runner

Why: the runner only calls the wrapper once it is set as its command_prefix. After this, every job writes a job_start and a job_end event.

Do: add the prefix to /etc/circleci-runner/circleci-runner-config.yaml on the runner host:

runner:
 command_prefix: ["/usr/local/bin/circleci-job-wrapper"]

Restart the runner. On the runner host:

sudo systemctl restart circleci-runner

Then run any job on it. In the CircleCI web app, rerun a workflow that uses this resource class.

Check: this proves the runner called the wrapper for your job and that the wrapper found the host and the resource class. After the job ends, on the runner host:

# the last two events, with the fields that matter
tail -n2 /var/log/circleci-job-wrapper/jobs.jsonl |
 jq -c '{event,job_id,trace_id,runner_name,
 instance_id,resource_class,agent_status}'

Expected output (one line per event, wrapped here):

{"event":"job_start","job_id":"5b1e0c1a-0000-4000-8000-000000000001",
 "trace_id":"9f8e7d6c5b4a39281706f5e4d3c2b1a0",
 "runner_name":"runner-a","instance_id":"i-0123456789abcdef0",
 "resource_class":"my-org/linux-large","agent_status":""}
{"event":"job_end","job_id":"5b1e0c1a-0000-4000-8000-000000000001",
 "trace_id":"9f8e7d6c5b4a39281706f5e4d3c2b1a0",
 "runner_name":"runner-a","instance_id":"i-0123456789abcdef0",
 "resource_class":"my-org/linux-large","agent_status":"completed"}

Both events are present, job_id is a UUID, and instance_id and resource_class are filled.

If it fails: if the file is empty or missing, see jobs.jsonl is missing or empty. If instance_id is empty, see EC2 fields are empty.

4. Turn on CircleCI’s OpenTelemetry export

Why: the wrapper knows the host. CircleCI knows the job result, the steps and their timing. You get those as OpenTelemetry spans, from an exporter you add once per organization.

Do: add the exporter in the CircleCI web app (option A) or with the API (option B). It needs organization admin rights, and CircleCI supports up to 5 exporters per organization. Spans are sent when each job finishes.

If your collector restricts source IPs, allow CircleCI’s core IPs. List them with dig core.knownips.circleci.com. Grafana Cloud needs no allow-list.

Official documentation: OpenTelemetry integration and the API reference.

Grafana Cloud values

Setting Value
Endpoint https://otlp-gateway-<region>.grafana.net/otlp/v1/traces
Protocol http
Header Authorization: Basic <base64 of instance-id:token>

On your workstation, build the header value:

printf '%s' '<instance-id>:<token>' | base64 -w0

Note

<region> is the region of your stack. Take it from your data source URLs or from the OTLP tile of your stack. It is not necessarily the region embedded in the token.

Option A: the CircleCI web app

In the CircleCI web app:

  1. Open Organization settings, then OpenTelemetry Configuration.
  2. Choose Add exporter.
  3. Pick the protocol (http), enter the endpoint, and add the header.
  4. Save.

Option B: the API

Use an organization admin personal API token. On your workstation:

curl -sS -X POST https://circleci.com/api/v2/otel/exporters \
 -H "Circle-Token: $CIRCLECI_TOKEN" \
 -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
 -d '{
 "org_id": "<your-org-id>",
 "endpoint": "https://otlp-gateway-<region>.grafana.net/otlp/v1/traces",
 "protocol": "http",
 "headers": {"Authorization": "Basic <base64 of instance-id:token>"}
 }'

Datadog and other OTLP backends

Any backend that takes OTLP over HTTP works the same way: use its OTLP traces endpoint, protocol http, and the header it documents for authentication. For Datadog, that means an Agent or Collector that accepts OTLP, with its API key header. This is not tested here.

What spans you get

Span What it covers
pipeline The pipeline run
workflow One workflow of the pipeline
job One job
task The task that executes the job
step One step, named Step: <name>, with its duration, its result (com.circleci.task.result) and its exit code (com.circleci.step.exit_code)

Attributes you will use:

  • com.circleci.job.id: equals the wrapper’s job_id. This is the join key.
  • com.circleci.job.status: the job result.
  • com.circleci.resource.class: the resource class.
  • vcs.ref.head.name: the branch.
  • The trace ID is the pipeline ID without dashes. It equals the wrapper’s trace_id.

The spans carry no CPU or memory and no host identity. The wrapper adds the host and the job’s CPU time, and the shipper in stage 5 adds host and cgroup metrics.

Check: this proves CircleCI is exporting spans, that your backend accepts them, and that the join key reaches Tempo. Run a job on the runner and wait for it to finish. Then in the Grafana web app, open Explore, pick your Tempo data source and run this TraceQL query:

{ span.com.circleci.job.id != "" }

Expected output: a list of traces, one per job, such as:

Trace ID Start time Name
9f8e7d6c5b4a39281706f5e4d3c2b1a0 2026-11-18 20:31:55 workflow build

Open one: it has a job span whose com.circleci.job.id equals the job_id you saw in stage 3.

If it fails: re-check the stack region and the header, and the exporter list in OpenTelemetry Configuration. Spans can take a minute to appear. See Join data with CircleCI OpenTelemetry.

5. Install and configure the shipper

Why: the shipper moves jobs.jsonl, host metrics and per-job CPU and memory to your backend. This guide uses Grafana Alloy, the tested example. The Datadog Agent is documented but not tested.

Do: install Alloy by following Grafana’s instructions, then configure it. On the runner host:

# env file of the alloy service, for example /etc/default/alloy
sudo tee -a /etc/default/alloy >/dev/null <<'ENV'
OTLP_ENDPOINT=https://otlp-gateway-<region>.grafana.net/otlp
OTLP_USERNAME=<instance-id>
OTLP_PASSWORD=<access-token>
EC2_INSTANCE_ID=<this host's instance id>
ENV
sudo chmod 0640 /etc/default/alloy

# let alloy read the log, the textfile directory, the journal
sudo usermod -aG circleci,systemd-journal alloy

sudo install -m 0644 examples/alloy/config.alloy \
 /etc/alloy/config.alloy
sudo systemctl restart alloy

Replace circleci with the runner’s group. The endpoint here has no /v1/traces: Alloy exports logs and metrics, not traces. Never commit the token.

What each block of examples/alloy/config.alloy does:

  1. Wrapper events. Tails jobs.jsonl, promotes event, resource_class, runner and instance_id to labels and sends the lines as OTLP logs.
  2. Task-agent journal (optional, experimental). Keeps four log messages from the runner units for live step progress and the host-side job result.
  3. Host metrics. prometheus.exporter.unix for CPU, memory, disk and network, plus the busy gauge textfile.
  4. cAdvisor block. prometheus.exporter.cadvisor reads cgroup CPU and memory. A relabel rule keeps only the /system.slice/circleci-runner*.service cgroups and a few series. Each runner agent runs one job at a time, so its service cgroup is per-job CPU and memory over time. The wrapper’s cgroup field joins to it.
  5. EC2 identity. resourcedetection sets host.id, and a transform copies it into an instance_id attribute on metrics.
  6. Export. OTLP over HTTP with basic auth.

Check 5a: Alloy runs without errors. This proves the config loads and the shipper is running. On the runner host:

sudo systemctl is-active alloy
sudo journalctl -u alloy -n 20 --no-pager |
 grep -i error || echo "no errors"

Expected output:

active
no errors

If it fails: a permission error means alloy is not yet in the runner group, see Alloy cannot read the log or the journal. A 401 means the user or token in /etc/default/alloy is wrong.

Check 5b: your backend receives the logs and the metrics. This proves data arrives, not only that Alloy runs. In the Grafana web app, open Explore, pick the Loki data source and run:

{service_name="circleci-job-wrapper"}

Expected output: log lines, one per job event, such as {"schema":1,"event":"job_end", ...}. Then pick the Prometheus data source and run:

circleci_runner_busy

Expected output: one series per runner:

circleci_runner_busy{runner="runner-a",
 instance_id="i-0123456789abcdef0"} 0

container_cpu_usage_seconds_total{cgroup=~"/system.slice/circleci-runner.*"} should return series too.

If it fails: nothing in Loki means Alloy cannot read the log. Nothing for circleci_runner_busy means CCI_JOBLOG_PROM_DIR is unset (stage 2). See Ship with Grafana Alloy and Troubleshooting.

6. Import the dashboards

Why: the dashboards turn the events, spans and metrics into the fleet, job, runner and resource class views.

Do: find the UIDs of your data sources in the Grafana web app, under Connections, Data sources (the UID is in the URL). Then generate the dashboard JSON. On your workstation, from a checkout of this repository:

python3 examples/grafana/build_dashboard.py \
 --prom <prom-uid> --loki <loki-uid> --tempo <tempo-uid> \
 > dashboard.json
python3 examples/grafana/build_job_dashboard.py \
 --prom <prom-uid> --loki <loki-uid> --tempo <tempo-uid> \
 > job-dashboard.json

For CircleCI Server add --app-url https://<your-circleci-host> so links open your installation.

Import them either way:

  • In the Grafana web app: Dashboards, New, Import, upload each JSON file.

  • With the API, on your workstation:

    jq -n --slurpfile d dashboard.json \
 '{dashboard: $d[0], overwrite: true}' |
 curl -sS -X POST "$GRAFANA_URL/api/dashboards/db" \
 -H "Authorization: Bearer $GRAFANA_TOKEN" \
 -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d @-

    Repeat for job-dashboard.json.

The runner detail and resource class dashboards are generated the same way, see the dashboards page.

Check: this proves the dashboards import and can read your data. In the Grafana web app, open the CircleCI runner fleet dashboard and look at the Fleet right now row.

Expected output: the dashboard opens, and the row shows your runners as busy or idle, with a table of what each is running now. The tour shows what it looks like.

If it fails: a “No data” row means a data source UID is wrong or stage 5 is not shipping yet. Re-run the builder with the right UIDs, and see Troubleshooting.

7. Verify the join

Why: this proves the three sources meet for one job: the wrapper (host), CircleCI spans (result and steps) and the shipper (CPU and memory).

Do: in the Grafana web app:

  1. On the fleet dashboard, open Recent jobs and pick a job.
  2. Click Drill into this job. The job-detail dashboard opens, already filtered to that job.

Check: confirm you see the following. Each item matches an image in the tour: the first two are in the job trace image (4), the last two in the steps and resources image (5).

  • Where and when it ran: the instance, runner, resource class and cgroup, from the wrapper.
  • The trace: pipeline, workflow, job and steps, from CircleCI spans.
  • Steps, slowest first, each with its step status (ok or failed, from the span status) and its exit code (com.circleci.step.exit_code).
  • Resources used during this job: CPU and memory of the runner’s cgroup, the job’s CPU time, and host metrics.

Expected output: all four are filled. For example, the where-and-when panel shows:

instance i-0123456789abcdef0
runner runner-a
resource my-org/linux-large
job status success

If it fails: if the trace panel is empty, the span export (stage 4) is the usual cause. Check the exporter, then that trace_id in the wrapper event equals the trace ID in Tempo. If the CPU panels are empty, check the cAdvisor block (stage 5) and the cgroup value in the event. See Troubleshooting.

You now have the full setup. Example Grafana dashboards describes every panel, Several runners, upgrades and removal covers day-two tasks, and Troubleshooting covers the common failures.

item.title: Troubleshooting
item.description:
The wrapper never fails a job over logging, so a problem usually shows up as missing data, not as an error. Turn on diagnostics first: set CCI_JOBLOG_DEBUG=1 in the runner service environment, restart the runner, and read the runner’s journal.

jobs.jsonl is missing or empty

  1. Check that the runner uses the wrapper: command_prefix in the runner config must be ["/usr/local/bin/circleci-job-wrapper"], and the runner must have been restarted after the change.
  2. Check that the file is executable: ls -l /usr/local/bin/circleci-job-wrapper.
  3. Check that CCI_JOBLOG_DISABLE is not set in the runner’s environment.
  4. Check the permissions below.

Permission denied on the log directory

The wrapper appends as the runner user, and skips logging silently if it cannot write. Check that /var/log/circleci-job-wrapper is writable by that user:

sudo -u circleci test -w /var/log/circleci-job-wrapper && echo writable

Replace circleci with your runner user. Fix it with a group-writable directory (mode 0775, owned by the runner group), or a Group= drop-in for the host cache unit. If logrotate recreated the file as root, switch to copytruncate as in the shipped config.

EC2 fields are empty

  • Check that IMDS is enabled on the instance, and that you are on EC2. See EC2 metadata.
  • Check the cache: cat /run/circleci-job-wrapper/host.env (it contains the instance identity, not secrets). If the unit failed, run systemctl status circleci-job-wrapper-hostcache.service.
  • A negative result is cached for 300 s. After you fix IMDS, run sudo /usr/local/bin/circleci-job-wrapper --refresh-host-cache.

runner_name is empty or the state file is called pid-NNN.json

The wrapper could not find runner.name. Set CCI_RUNNER_NAME in the runner’s environment or the operator file, or check that the runner config has a name: key directly under runner:. See Configuration.

resource_class is empty

The runner does not tell the wrapper its resource class. Set CCI_RESOURCE_CLASS in the operator file. See Configuration.

A job_start has no job_end

This is expected when the runner kills the wrapper with SIGKILL. See How it works. Treat a state file whose wrapper_pid is gone as stale.

Alloy cannot read the log or the journal

  • Add the alloy user to the runner’s group so it can read jobs.jsonl, and restart Alloy.
  • For the journal pipeline, add alloy to the systemd-journal group.
  • Make the CCI_JOBLOG_PROM_DIR directory readable by alloy.
  • Check that matches in config.alloy lists your runner units.

Then read the Alloy log for permission denied or no such file.

item.title: EC2 metadata
item.description:
The wrapper reads the instance identity from one request to the instance identity document (/latest/dynamic/instance-identity/document).

  • The instance metadata service (IMDS) must be enabled on the instance. On non-EC2 hosts, or with IMDS disabled, the EC2 fields are empty and nothing else changes.
  • IMDSv2 works and is recommended (HttpTokens=required). The wrapper sends PUT /latest/api/token first and falls back to IMDSv1 only if that fails. Timeouts are 0.3 s to connect and 1 s in total per request, and proxies are bypassed.
  • A hop limit of 1 is enough for jobs that run on the host, because the wrapper runs on the host itself. Use a hop limit of 2 only if the jobs themselves, for example containers they start, query IMDS.
  • Instance metadata tags (InstanceMetadataTags=enabled) are optional and the wrapper does not read them. To put a tag such as Team on every event, read it once at boot (/latest/meta-data/tags/instance/<key>) and write it to CCI_JOBLOG_EXTRA_FIELDS in the operator file.

Cache

The identity is cached in CCI_JOBLOG_HOST_CACHE (tmpfs by default) together with the kernel boot id, so a cache that survives in an image or a new boot is ignored.

The boot-time unit (circleci-job-wrapper --refresh-host-cache, 3 attempts) fills the cache, so no job ever queries IMDS. Without the unit, the first job on each boot fills it, while the job runs and never delaying its start. If the cache cannot be written, each job queries IMDS itself. A negative result (not on EC2) is cached for 300 s.

item.title: How it works
item.description:
How command_prefix invokes the wrapper

With this runner config:

runner:
 command_prefix: ["/usr/local/bin/circleci-job-wrapper"]

the runner executes

/usr/local/bin/circleci-job-wrapper <task-agent-path> <agent args...>

with the job’s built-in environment (CIRCLE_*) added and the task token on stdin. The wrapper:

  1. Starts the task agent as a child with <&0, so stdin is the very same pipe.
  2. While the job already runs, resolves the host identity and writes job_start and the state file. The cost to job start-up is one fork.
  3. Waits for the child. If the wrapper itself gets SIGTERM, SIGINT or SIGHUP, it forwards the signal to the child.
  4. Writes job_end, removes the state file, and exits with the child’s exit code (128+n for a signalled child).

Every helper command the wrapper runs has </dev/null, so it can never take the task token from the agent’s stdin. The wrapper never changes the job’s environment, umask or process group.

Overhead

About 6 ms per job. The agent is spawned before any telemetry runs. Logging is best effort: every logging failure is swallowed, and the wrapper is silent unless CCI_JOBLOG_DEBUG is set. It needs bash 4 or later and POSIX utilities, with no jq, no daemon and no Python.

agent_status is not the job result

The task agent exits 0 even when the job fails or is cancelled from the UI. So completed only means the agent process exited 0. Take the job result from the CircleCI span (com.circleci.job.status) or, on the host, from the task agent’s own “Reporting task end.” log line (see Ship with Grafana Alloy).

cancelled only means the wrapper received TERM, INT or HUP, for example because the runner is stopping a task.

Signals

When the runner stops a task, it sends SIGTERM to the command_prefix process only, not the process group. It sends SIGKILL to the whole process group after 10 s, or immediately with enable_unsafe_retries. So:

  • Signal forwarding (on by default) is required. Otherwise the agent never sees the SIGTERM.
  • If the agent has not exited within 10 s, the wrapper is killed too and job_end is lost. Consumers must tolerate a job_start without a job_end.
  • A cancel from the CircleCI UI is handled by the agent itself (exit 0, no signal), so it shows as completed.

stdin

The task token stays on the agent’s stdin. The wrapper never reads or redirects it.

Environment the runner provides

Verified on machine runner 3.1.14, these built-in variables reach the command_prefix process (names only):

CIRCLE_BRANCH CIRCLE_BUILD_NUM CIRCLE_BUILD_URL CIRCLE_JOB CIRCLE_NODE_INDEX CIRCLE_NODE_TOTAL CIRCLE_ORGANIZATION_ID CIRCLE_PIPELINE_ID CIRCLE_PROJECT_ID CIRCLE_PROJECT_REPONAME CIRCLE_PROJECT_USERNAME CIRCLE_REPOSITORY_URL CIRCLE_SHA1 CIRCLE_USERNAME CIRCLE_WORKFLOW_ID CIRCLE_WORKFLOW_JOB_ID CIRCLE_WORKFLOW_WORKSPACE_ID

There is no resource class, pipeline number or PR number, so those event fields stay empty unless you supply them. For the resource class, see Configuration.

Multiple runners on one host

Several runner agents share one wrapper, one log file and one cache. Each event carries its runner_name, and each runner has its own state file. See Several runners, upgrades and removal.

item.title: Several runners, upgrades and removal
item.description:
Day-two tasks for the wrapper after you have followed Set it up end to end.

Several runner agents on one host

Agents on one host share the wrapper, the log file and the cache. This was tested with two systemd units (circleci-runner and circleci-runner-b), each with its own -c config file and runner.name. The wrapper reads the name from the parent’s -c or --config argument, so nothing more is needed, and events from both interleave safely. Each runner has its own state file.

Set CCI_RUNNER_NAME in a unit’s environment only to override the name.

Check which runner wrote which event. On the runner host:

# one line per runner name seen in the last 200 events
tail -n 200 /var/log/circleci-job-wrapper/jobs.jsonl |
 jq -r .runner_name | sort | uniq -c

Expected output:

 12 runner-a
 9 runner-b

If it fails: a runner with an empty name is covered in Troubleshooting.

File locations and permissions

Path Mode and owner What it is
/usr/local/bin/circleci-job-wrapper 0755, root The wrapper
/var/log/circleci-job-wrapper/ 0775, root, runner group jobs.jsonl and its rotations. The runner user must be able to write here
/run/circleci-job-wrapper/ 1777 (sticky) State files and the root-owned host.env cache. Runner accounts write state files but cannot replace host.env
/etc/circleci-job-wrapper/wrapper.env 0644, root Operator settings. Parsed, never sourced
/etc/systemd/system/circleci-job-wrapper-hostcache.service 0644, root Boot-time host cache unit
/etc/logrotate.d/circleci-job-wrapper 0644, root Daily rotation

The host cache unit runs circleci-job-wrapper --refresh-host-cache once per boot and creates the two directories above. If your runner group is not circleci, add a Group= line in a drop-in of the unit.

Upgrade the wrapper

The wrapper is one file, and each job starts a fresh copy, so an upgrade needs no downtime. A job that is running keeps using the old copy. On the runner host, from an updated checkout:

# replace the script atomically
sudo install -m 0755 bin/circleci-job-wrapper \
 /usr/local/bin/circleci-job-wrapper.new
sudo mv /usr/local/bin/circleci-job-wrapper.new \
 /usr/local/bin/circleci-job-wrapper

# refresh the unit and logrotate files if they changed
sudo install -m 0644 systemd/circleci-job-wrapper-hostcache.service \
 /etc/systemd/system/
sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo systemctl restart circleci-job-wrapper-hostcache.service

Check that the new version works. Run a job, then:

tail -n1 /var/log/circleci-job-wrapper/jobs.jsonl | jq -c '{event,schema}'

Expected output:

{"event":"job_end","schema":1}

If it fails: see Troubleshooting. To roll back, install the previous copy the same way.

Uninstall

Remove the prefix first, so no job calls a missing file. On the runner host:

# 1. delete the command_prefix lines from the runner config, then
sudo systemctl restart circleci-runner

# 2. remove the wrapper, the unit, rotation and settings
sudo systemctl disable --now circleci-job-wrapper-hostcache.service
sudo rm /etc/systemd/system/circleci-job-wrapper-hostcache.service
sudo rm /etc/logrotate.d/circleci-job-wrapper
sudo rm /usr/local/bin/circleci-job-wrapper
sudo rm -r /etc/circleci-job-wrapper
sudo systemctl daemon-reload

The logs in /var/log/circleci-job-wrapper stay until you delete them.

Run the tests

make check runs shellcheck and the bats tests. It needs bats, jq, python3 and curl. strace and iconv are used when present.

item.title: Ship with Grafana Alloy
item.description:
examples/alloy/config.alloy ships the wrapper events, the optional task-agent journal lines and host metrics to any OTLP/HTTP endpoint. It is tested with Grafana Cloud. The end-to-end guide walks through the install. Its blocks:

  1. File tail to Loki over OTLP. local.file_match and loki.source.file tail jobs.jsonl. loki.process promotes event, resource_class, runner and instance_id to labels. Job and workflow IDs stay in the JSON body, queried with | json. otelcol.receiver.loki and otelcol.processor.transform turn the stream into OTLP logs named circleci-job-wrapper.
  2. Journal pipeline (optional, experimental). loki.source.journal reads the runner units’ journal. The task agent writes JSON lines there. loki.process keeps only Runner started execution, step start, step end and Reporting task end. (each has a job-id) and labels them event=task_start|step_start|step_end|task_end, log_type=task_agent and instance_id. This gives near-real-time step progress and the job result per host. It is an internal format and may change between runner versions. Edit matches to list your runner units.
  3. Host metrics. prometheus.exporter.unix with its textfile collector pointed at CCI_JOBLOG_PROM_DIR, scraped every 15 s into otelcol.receiver.prometheus.
  4. Per-job CPU and memory (cAdvisor). prometheus.exporter.cadvisor reads cgroup CPU, memory and disk IO. prometheus.relabel keeps only the /system.slice/circleci-runner*.service cgroups and a few series, and copies the cgroup into a cgroup label. Each runner agent runs one job at a time, so this is per-job usage. Join it with the wrapper’s cgroup field.
  5. EC2 identity. otelcol.processor.resourcedetection with the ec2 and system detectors sets host.id (the instance ID) on logs and metrics.
  6. instance_id on metrics. otelcol.processor.transform "metrics" copies host.id into an instance_id datapoint attribute, so metrics join with the wrapper’s instance_id.
  7. Export. otelcol.exporter.otlphttp with otelcol.auth.basic.

Environment

For example in /etc/default/alloy:

Variable Meaning
OTLP_ENDPOINT OTLP/HTTP base URL. For Grafana Cloud, the stack’s region gateway, https://otlp-gateway-<region>.grafana.net/otlp
OTLP_USERNAME Grafana Cloud instance (stack) ID
OTLP_PASSWORD Access token with write scope. Never commit it
EC2_INSTANCE_ID This host’s instance ID, used for the journal lines. Write it at install time from IMDSv2 (/latest/meta-data/instance-id)

Permissions

The alloy user needs read access to jobs.jsonl: add it to the runner’s group. The journal pipeline also needs membership of systemd-journal. The textfile directory must be readable by alloy too.

CircleCI spans to Grafana

Send CircleCI’s OpenTelemetry spans to the same stack with CircleCI’s exporter API (POST /api/v2/otel/exporters):

  • Endpoint: the gateway URL above with /v1/traces appended.
  • Protocol: http.
  • Header: Authorization: Basic <base64(stackid:token)>.

The spans then land in Tempo, with com.circleci.job.id matching the wrapper’s job_id.

item.title: Security
item.description:
To report a vulnerability, read SECURITY.md.

What the wrapper reads and writes

  • Allow-list only. The wrapper reads fixed CIRCLE_* names, the host identity and the operator settings. Tokens (CIRCLE_TOKEN and similar), the environment and the agent’s arguments are never read into a log call.
  • The runner config is read only to find runner.name. The auth token line is not kept, logged or used. /proc/<parent>/cmdline is read only to find the --config path.
  • Operator files and the cache are parsed as key=value, never sourced.
  • The task token stays on the agent’s stdin. The wrapper never reads or redirects it, and all helper commands run with </dev/null.
  • Job-controlled text (branch names, job names) is escaped and length-capped (256 bytes by default, never splitting a UTF-8 character). A line that is still over 3800 bytes is replaced by a minimal one.
  • The HTTP header travels to curl on stdin, never in ps. The IMDS token is short-lived (60 s) and used only for the request. Use HTTPS for the sink.
  • The job keeps its environment, umask and process group.

What you should decide

  • The log is world-readable by default (0644, as created by the first writer) and contains project, branch and user-controlled strings. Restrict the directory if that matters.
  • /run/circleci-job-wrapper is sticky and mode 1777, like /tmp, so runner users cannot delete each other’s state files or replace the root-owned host.env. Tighten it (for example 0775 with a Group=) if all runners share one account.
  • Signal forwarding is what lets the agent shut down cleanly, because the runner sends SIGTERM to the wrapper only. Set CCI_JOBLOG_FORWARD_SIGNALS=0 only if you must.
  • Extra fields skip keys that look like secrets, but only the operator should write the operator file.

item.title: Ship with Datadog Agent
item.description:
Warning

This is documented but not tested in this repository.

See Datadog’s custom log collection and Prometheus host collection.

  1. Enable logs in datadog.yaml: logs_enabled: true.

  2. Create /etc/datadog-agent/conf.d/circleci_job_wrapper.d/conf.yaml:

    logs:
 - type: file
 path: /var/log/circleci-job-wrapper/jobs.jsonl
 service: circleci-job-wrapper
 source: circleci

    Datadog parses the JSON into attributes. Make @job_id, @instance_id and @runner_name facets.

  3. Add the dd-agent user to the runner’s group so it can read the file.

  4. Optional: add a second type: journald source for the runner units, with include_units, to get the task agent’s step and result lines. The same caveat applies: the format is internal.

  5. Host metrics come from the Agent’s built-in system checks. On EC2, the host is identified by its instance ID.

  6. For the busy gauge, point the Agent’s OpenMetrics check at node_exporter’s textfile collector, or build Datadog log-based metrics from job_start and job_end.

  7. CircleCI spans reach Datadog through its OTLP intake (the Agent’s or a Collector’s OTLP receiver, or Datadog’s OTLP endpoint), using the same CircleCI exporter API as in Ship with Grafana Alloy.

item.title: FAQ
item.description:
Does it change my jobs?

No. The task agent runs as a normal child. Stdin is the same pipe, signals are forwarded, and the exit status is returned exactly. If logging fails, the job does not.

Does it slow jobs down?

About 6 ms per job. The agent starts before any telemetry runs.

Do I need OpenTelemetry or Grafana?

No. The wrapper writes jobs.jsonl with nothing else. The OpenTelemetry export, a shipper and the dashboard are optional. See what you need.

Is the agent_status the job result?

No. See How it works. Take the result from the CircleCI span or the task-agent journal.

Does it work off EC2?

Yes. The EC2 fields are empty and everything else works.

Does it work with CircleCI Server, container runner, Windows or macOS?

Not tested and not supported. The project targets machine runner 3.1.11 or later on Linux. CCI_JOBLOG_APP_URL exists for CircleCI Server links, but that setup was not tested.

Why a wrapper, and not only CircleCI’s OpenTelemetry spans?

The spans carry the job result and timing, but no runner or host identity. The wrapper adds the host. If CircleCI later adds that to the built-in runner telemetry, you may not need this project.

Why is the task-agent journal pipeline experimental?

It reads the task agent’s internal log lines, and that format may change between runner versions.

Can I send events to another system?

Yes. Ship jobs.jsonl with any log shipper (Vector, Fluent Bit and others), or set CCI_JOBLOG_HTTP_URL to POST every event.

Where do I ask for help?

See Support on the home page.
